title: Birha: the ache of separation
hookLine: Guru Ram Das's hymns long for the sight of the Beloved and the True Guru (Sri Rag M4, ang 40)
carry: longing for darsan is part of the road

cards: What does missing someone actually want? Not news. You can know everything about a person far away, what they ate, where they went, how the weather is, and the ache stays exactly where it was.
What it wants is to see them. The face. The door opening, and there they are.

Earlier on this path we heard young Arjan's letters home, longing to see his father. Now we hear the father. Guru Ram Das has hymns full of that same ache, and the word at the center of them is sight.

teach.h: BIRHA: THE ACHE OF BEING APART.
teach.b: One, from Sri Rag, paraphrased. In my mind and body, the pain of separation is great. How will my Beloved come home and meet me?
When I see my Lord, seeing him, the pain goes away. I go and ask my friends: how can I meet the Lord? And the refrain: O my True Guru, without you I have no other.
Four things are in there. First, the word for that pain, birha, the ache of being apart from someone you love. The hymn doesn't hide it or hurry past it.
It's great, and it's in the mind and the body both. Second, the cure. Not a better argument.
Sikhs call that seeing darsan: a glimpse of the beloved, of the Guru, of the Lord.

teach.h: ASK THE FRIENDS WHO HAVE MET.
teach.b: Third, the friends. Longing doesn't sit alone at home. It goes out and asks the people who have met the Beloved how they did it.
That's one picture of what the sangat is for.

teach.h: WITHOUT YOU, I HAVE NO OTHER.
teach.b: Fourth, the refrain turns to the Guru: without you, I have no other.

The longing for God and for the Guru run through the same hymn, because in Sikh teaching it's the Guru who shows the way to that sight. And the hymn trusts the longing. It's not a problem to get over.
The ache is part of the road. It's what sends you out the door, asking.

how: Sikhs speak of going for darsan of the Guru Granth Sahib at the gurdwara and of the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, and Guru Ram Das's hymns of longing are sung in kirtan.

o: the ache of separation, healed by seeing the Beloved
a prayer to heal blindness and failing eyes
the wish to see visions and miracles in prayer

games.q: the hymn of longing: tap the pairs.
p: asked how to meet the Lord
without you, I have no other

s: the hymn treats longing as something to get over quickly
it names the pain as great and lets it send the singer out asking.
in the hymn, seeing the Lord takes the pain away
when I see my Lord, the pain goes.
the refrain is addressed to the True Guru
O my True Guru, without you I have no other.

games.q: the ache of separation is great, in mind and body. what does the singer of the hymn do next?
o: stays home and waits it out.
goes and asks friends how to meet the Lord.
games.why: I go and ask my friends: how can I meet the Lord? longing goes looking for company.

practice: Find a photo of the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the gurdwara Sikhs travel to for darsan, and just look: the water, the reflection, the people walking around.
If you can't find one, let a place or a face you long to see come to mind instead, and look at it gently, with no need to fix the longing. If you pray, let Waheguru keep it company.

wordCard.voice: Longing for sight. Guru Ram Das's ache of separation, healed by seeing: darsan of the Beloved, and the True Guru without whom there is no other. Today's word.

orig.note: sight, a glimpse of the beloved: of the Guru, of the Lord; what the longing in these hymns wants.

carryVoice: Your line: longing for darsan is part of the road. The ache knows the way. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Rag Mahala 4, Ang 40 (in mind and body the pain of separation is great; when I see the Lord the pain goes; I ask my friends how to meet the Lord; O my True Guru, without you I have no other)
